sentences.text: Briefly stated, the case of the prosecution against the accused is that on 17.03.2016 at 05:45 PM in front of back gate of Milan Vihar, Delhi, the accused was found driving a car Honda Amaze bearing No. HR 26CF 8315 in a rash and negligent manner and while driving the said car, the accused hit the nephew of complainant Vikram Gupta and caused grievous injuries to him.

As such, it is alleged that the accused committed the offence under Sections 279/338 IPC of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter, "IPC") for which FIR No. 200/2016 was registered at Police Station Madhu Vihar,
Delhi.
INVESTIGATION AND APPEARANCE OF ACCUSED 2.

On culmination of the investigation, chargesheet against the accused namely Rohit Sharma for the alleged commission of offences u/s 279/338 IPC was filed.
Ld. Predecessor of this Court took cognizance of the offence vide order dated 28.08.2018.

After taking cognizance of the offence, accused appeared in Court and he was supplied the copy of documents relied upon in the charge sheet in terms of section 207 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter,
"CrPC").

sentences.text: The gravamen of the offence under section 279/338 IPC is the act of accused, done with "rashness" or "negligence".
The IPC does not define either of these terms.
However, the ambit of these terms has now been settled by judicial pronouncements from time to time.

15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Rathnashavlvan vs. State of Karnataka (2007)
3 SCC 474 has observed, inter alia, as under:
"7. .... Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper precautions and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.

entities.text:
Rathnashavlvan vs. State of Karnataka (2007)
3 SCC 474
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Rashness means doing an act with the consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.
Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors.

A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of precaution and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.

Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.
8. As noted above, "rashness" consists in hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so, and that it may cause injury.
The criminality lies in such a case in running the risk of doing such an act with recklessness or indifference as to the consequences.

Criminal negligence on Digitally signed by FIR No.200/2016 State State vs Rohit Sharma on 2 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/194874346/

the other hand, is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which, having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge has arisen it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted."
16.

Similar observations were made by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sushil Ansal vs.
CBI (2014) 6 SCC 173.

The standard of negligence was discussed in the said case, by observing, inter alia, as under: -
"58.

In the case of "negligence" the courts have favoured a meaning which implies a gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual which having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge arises, it may be the imperative duty of the accused to have adopted.

Negligence has been understood to be an omission to do something which a reasonable man guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person would not do.

Unlike rashness, where the immutability arises from acting despite the consciousness,
negligence implies acting without such consciousness, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him.
The immutability in the case of negligence arises from the neglect of the civil duty of circumspection."

17. In S.N. Hussain v. State of A.P., (1972) 3 SCC 18, the Hon'ble Supreme Court while discussing rashness and criminal negligence observed:
"9. ... Rashness consists in hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so, and that it may cause injury.

Criminal negligence on the other hand, is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which,
having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge hasarisen, it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted..."

Thus, rashness implies doing an act despite consciousness that it might result in injuries,
negligence, on the other hand, means lack of reasonable precautions that a person placed in the effect situation ought to take, in order to avoid injuries.

The general burden of proof, which is a non-shifting burden, on the prosecution is to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by adducing cogent evidence that point only towards the guilt of accused.
The evidence in the present case is to be weighed keeping in view the above legal standards.
APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE 20.

After going through the testimonies of all the witnesses, following are the issues/facts that have erupted which raise doubts on the version of prosecution:
a.
The injured of the case Anmol Mani expired during the pendency of the matter and he could not be examined in the case so as to substantiate the case of prosecution.
b. There are material contradictions in the testimony of PW-1 as he deposed two different dates and two different times of the alleged incident in his examination-in-chief and cross- examination.

c. It is the case of the prosecution that PW-1 was the eyewitness of the case however,
in his cross-examination he deposed that there were other persons also present on the spot but none of them was made as a witness in the present case.

d. Presence of the witness PW-1 at the time of incident is also not confirmed since he deposed that in his cross-examination that his duty hours were 9 am to 6 pm whereas the alleged incident was of 5:45 pm which creates doubts as to his presence on the spot.
Absence of any other ocular or documentary evidence State vs. Rohit Sharma Udbhav Kumar Jain by Udbhav

. Mere statement by PW-1 that the accused was driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner does not prove that that accused had the required intent or his conduct was such that the ingredients of the offence are satisfied.
22. Thus, there are material contradictions in the case of prosecution which are fatal to the case of prosecution itself.
The nature of burden of proof to prove the guilt of accused is beyond reasonable doubt but the accused has been successful in raising doubt on the version of prosecution.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
After going through the record and considering the material available on record, the only point of determination that is left is whether the prosecution has been able to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Udbhav
In order to prove the offences punishable under section 279 and 338 IPC, the prosecution has to prove beyond reasonable doubt, the following mandatory ingredients:
a) That accident actually took place;
b) That a vehicle was driven or ridden by the accused at the time of accident;
c) That the accused was driving it on a public way; and d) The said vehicle was driven in a rash or negligent manner;
e) Such rash or negligent act of the accused leading to the accident caused grievous hurt to the injured.
14.
The gravamen of the offence under section 279/338 IPC is the act of accused, done with "rashness" or "negligence".
However, the ambit of these terms has now been settled by judicial pronouncements from time to time.
15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Rathnashavlvan vs. State of Karnataka (2007)
3 SCC 474 has observed, inter alia, as under:
"7. .... Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper precautions and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.
Rashness means doing an act with the consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.
Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors.
A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of precaution and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.
Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.

The general burden of proof, which is a non-shifting burden, on the prosecution is to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by adducing cogent evidence that point only towards the guilt of accused.
The evidence in the present case is to be weighed keeping in view the above legal standards.
The injured of the case Anmol Mani expired during the pendency of the matter and he could not be examined in the case so as to substantiate the case of prosecution.
Thus, testimony of PW-1 fails to inspire confidence so as to prove the case of prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
e. PW-1 has merely deposed that the accused was driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner, but it is not clear as to how the accused was driving the vehicle in such a manner.
Mere use of the words as provided in the provision does not make the accused guilty.
The presumption of innocence is in favour of the accused and for it to be rebutted, cogent evidence has to be led.

10 f.
It is not the case that the alleged incident took place behind closed doors and when the same was committed on a public road then why no public person who saw the alleged incident was neither examined nor made as a witness created adverse inference on the story of the prosecution itself.
There is no evidence in particular which connects the accused with alleged commission of offences.
It cannot be said without a reasonable doubt that accused was driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner and thereby caused injury to the nephew of the complainant.
Further nothing has come on record especially from the testimony of PW-1 that the accused was driving the vehicle recklessly or indifferently as to the consequences.
The nature of burden of proof to prove the guilt of accused is beyond reasonable doubt but the accused has been successful in raising doubt on the version of prosecution.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Dayabhai Chagganbhai Thakkar vs State of Gujarat AIR 1964 SC 1563, held that if the accused is able to raise doubt on the story of the prosecution, then it is clear that it is the prosecution who is not able to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt.
The same view was reiterated by the Hon'ble Apex Court recently in Nanjundappa & Anr. Vs. The State of Karnataka 2022 SCC OnLine SC 628.
Thus, accused Rohit Sharma is entitled to benefit of doubt.
